newsitem.title: PERU: No sign of early solution to Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: No sign of early solution to Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis entered its third day on Friday with no sign of an early solution for the 400 hostages held by leftist guerrillas threatening to kill them if the government does not meet their demands.

Inside the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, the captives, still clad in elegant clothes for the cocktail party that the rebels stormed on Tuesday, slept on the floor and made do with meagre supplies of food and water.

In the street outside, dozens of Peruvians held a candle-lit vigil through the night, while nearby residents put out Peruvian flags, and hundreds of police, family members and journalists played a tense waiting game with the approximately 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas inside.

"There are 24 million Peruvians who will not allow the lives of those kidnapped to be threatened. We condemn this kidnapping but at the same time look for a solution," said one of the vigil organisers, legislator Manuel Lajo.

Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, facing one of the most serious crises of his political career, promised in a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton that the safety of hostages would be his first priority in resolving the guerrilla siege.

"I want to assure your excellency that I am occupying myself permanently and jointly with my team to achieve a solution as soon as possible to this crisis, the principal objective being the safeguarding of the health and life of those who are inside," Fujimori wrote in the letter.

Fujimori, who ignored an ultimatum by the rebels for his presence on Wednesday, has held three emergency cabinet meetings but still not made a public statement to the Peruvian people since the crisis began.

On Thursday night, he held a one-hour emergency meeting with Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who arrived earlier in the day to help negotiate the crisis. The pair emerged stony-faced from the meeting at Government Palace in downtown Lima, but gave no comments.
The shocking attack has posed a tough dilemma for Fujimori as he juggles his domestically popular tough stance against guerrillas with competing political, economic and international pressures.
The heavily armed rebels released four more captives on Thursday as talks, mediated by the Red Cross, continued over the fate of those remaining.
The rebels have threatened to kill their captives, who include many high-ranking diplomats, businessmen and government officials, if Peru does not release up to 500 of their imprisoned comrades.

Meanwhile, Ecuadoran President Abdala Bucaram said in Quito on Thursday he was ready to grant asylum to the rebels. "We have stated clearly that if we can be of help, providing the Peruvian government asks for it, we would accede to that," Bucaram said when asked by journalists if Ecuador would give asylum to the guerrillas.

Red Cross officials supplied those inside the residence with food and medical equipment. Red Cross official Michel Minning, who is leading talks with the rebels, was also conducting the supply operation, which even included delivering three chess sets and 200 rosary chains to the hostages.

Four ambassadors, released on Wednesday, were also mediating between those inside the Japanese residence and the authorities outside, Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent told a news conference. The other "hostages on parole" were the ambassadors of Germany and Greece and a Peruvian ambassador.
Vincent has said both the hostages, all men since the release late on Tuesday of women captives, and the MRTA members were well and behaving in a restrained manner.
A letter faxed early on Wednesday from the residence to family members of hostages and signed by captives said there were 490 hostages. Six have been released since then.
The Red Cross put the number at 380.

Governments worldwide have urged Peru not to use force and to do everything in its power to protect the hostages. The embassy residence is legally Japanese territory, meaning in theory Fujimori would need Tokyo's approval for an assault.

The United States on Thursday sent a team of security advisers to Lima to assist the U.S. ambassador to Peru in the crisis, the State Department said. The ambassador and his deputy attended the reception, but left before the siege.

The rebels, including three non-Peruvians, assaulted the fortified compound from outside on Tuesday, linking up with comrades disguised as waiters inside a cocktail reception to celebrate the Japanese emperor's birthday, anti-terrorist police sources said. Cartridges were smuggled into the building beforehand among flowers and inside a Christmas cake.

The rebels released Fujimori's mother and sister, but were still believed to be holding one of his brothers. The president, the son of Japanese immigrants, reportedly had planned to attend the party but was delayed on a trip to the provinces.
The captives also include Peru's foreign minister, agriculture minister, supreme court president and the current and past chiefs of the anti-terrorism police.
Attempts by the MRTA and the previously better-known Shining Path to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
